items.title: Apple adds Mac permission controls aimed at AI agents that ask for full disk access
items.tldr: macOS 27.3 will split risky permissions into clearer settings and show when one app is controlling another, as AI agents push for deeper access.
items.summary_md: Apple says macOS 27.3 will split its old device-control and data-access setting into two: a 'System & App Protection Override' switch and a separate Accessibility setting. Users can make an app ask every time it needs access, and a new indicator shows when one app is driving another. Developers who truly need full disk access, such as backup tools, can apply for exceptions. The changes do not stop agents from asking for broad access; they make the grant more visible.

items.title: Uber describes a security layer that checks AI agent actions before they run
items.tldr: Uber's framework checks whether an agent's next step matches what the user asked for before it touches anything sensitive.
items.summary_md: Uber's framework, reported by InfoQ, compares each action an autonomous agent proposes with the user's original request. It checks permissions and stated purpose before sensitive steps, then logs the activity so security teams can review it later. This is a design write-up, not a product launch, and no performance figures were given.

items.title: Alibaba's Qwen4-Max moves from preview to a paid API
items.tldr: Alibaba's next flagship model takes text, images and video, reads up to 1 million tokens, and plugs into common coding tools.
items.summary_md: Qwen4-Max opened as a two-week preview on 11 November, available only through Alibaba's Token Plan subscription. It accepts text, images and video, has a 1-million-token context window (roughly 750,000 words), and can produce up to 393,216 output tokens. It speaks the OpenAI and Anthropic API formats, so tools like Claude Code, Cline and Codex can use it. Release trackers list a full API launch on 16 November at $1.50 per million input tokens and $4.50 per million output tokens. Alibaba has not published benchmarks, parameter count or open weights.

items.title: Gemini 4 Carbon tops the MathArena leaderboard, but at about 15 times GPT-6.1 Sol's cost
items.tldr: Google's top model now ranks first on a set of hard maths contests, but the tested setup was far more expensive and often ran out of time.
items.summary_md: MathArena tests models on fresh competition maths problems so they cannot have memorised the answers. Gemini 4 Carbon now ranks first, ahead of OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol. The tested configuration cost about 15 times more per evaluation than GPT-6.1 Sol and often went past the time limit. For most users, the cheaper model may still be the better buy.

items.title: A hand-drawn fish game pitched as 'no AI' becomes a surprise viral hit
items.tldr: In Drawquarium you draw your own fish, raise them, and keep the tank as a living desktop wallpaper, and players love it.
items.summary_md: Drawquarium, by developer Kaleb Lechowski, lets players doodle fish, feed them and build a cosy aquarium that can run as an animated wallpaper. It is marketed as made by humans, without generative AI. Its trailer drew more than 128,000 likes on one post and the game gained about 70,000 Steam wishlists in a week. The full game was due on 13 November, though unofficial copies of the demo have already appeared on Google Play.

sections.name: AI in Cardiac Surgery, Robotics & AI Models

items.title: AI reads heart risk from ordinary chest X-rays about as well as the PREVENT score, RSNA preview says
items.tldr: A Harvard-led team found that AI scores pulled from routine chest X-rays predicted heart attacks and strokes almost as well as a standard risk calculator, and better when the two were combined.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
Jay Chandra and colleagues will present a study at RSNA 2026 (30 November, Chicago) showing that deep-learning models can estimate heart risk from plain chest X-rays. They used nearly 40,000 patients from the National Lung Screening Trial and the Mass General Brigham Biobank. The AI scores were compared with PREVENT, the American Heart Association's 10-year risk equation.

## Why it matters
PREVENT needs blood tests such as cholesterol and kidney function. In emergency departments or one-off visits those results are often missing, but a chest X-ray is very common. A risk signal hidden in an image that already exists could flag people who would otherwise never be screened.

## How it works
Convolutional neural networks (CNNs, image-reading AI) estimated two things from each X-ray: a coronary artery calcium (CAC) score and a set of radiomic features (quantitative patterns of heart shape and texture).
- For detecting any calcium, the X-ray model reached an AUROC of up to 0.80.
- For predicting future major adverse cardiac events (MACE), the C-index was 0.65 for X-ray radiomics, 0.64 for predicted CAC, and 0.66 for PREVENT alone.
- Adding the X-ray scores to PREVENT raised the C-index to 0.71.
- Among people PREVENT called low risk (under 5%), those in the top radiomics quartile had about four times the event rate of the bottom quartile.

## Caveats
This is a conference preview, not a peer-reviewed paper, so full methods are not yet public. A C-index of 0.65 is modest; it ranks risk better than chance but is far from perfect. Both datasets are US cohorts, and lung-screening participants are older smokers, so results may not carry over to other groups. No study yet shows that acting on these scores improves outcomes.

## Key terms
- **Coronary artery calcium (CAC):** calcium deposits in heart arteries, a marker of plaque.
- **PREVENT:** AHA equation estimating 10-year cardiovascular risk from age, labs and other factors.
- **C-index / AUROC:** 0.5 means chance, 1.0 means perfect ranking of who has the outcome.
- **Radiomics:** numerical features extracted from medical images.
- **MACE:** major adverse cardiac events, such as heart attack, stroke or cardiac death.

items.title: Fine-tuning an adult ECG foundation model on 339,563 children's ECGs beats direct transfer and helps doctors
items.tldr: Adapting an adult ECG AI to children lifted its accuracy from an AUC of 0.83 to 0.97, and clinicians reading with it got more answers right.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
A Chinese team led by Haomin Li took an ECG foundation model trained on adult data and tested three ways to use it on children: as is, fine-tuned on pediatric ECGs, or trained from scratch with the same architecture. They used 339,563 standard 12-lead ECGs from 238,189 children, plus 10,999 ECGs from an outside site.

## Why it matters
Children's hearts differ from adults' in rate, size and normal ECG patterns, and pediatric cardiology expertise is scarce. Pediatric datasets are also small. If an adult model can be adapted cheaply, hospitals could get useful pediatric ECG tools without huge new labelling projects.

## How it works
A foundation model is a large network pretrained on broad data that can be adapted to new tasks. Here it was tested on many diagnostic labels.
- Used directly on children, the adult model reached a mean AUC of 0.826.
- Fine-tuned on pediatric data, it reached 0.970, slightly above training from scratch (0.966).
- With only 1% of the pediatric training data, fine-tuning still reached 0.908, which shows the value of adult pretraining when data are scarce.
- On the external dataset the mean AUC was 0.939 across 30 labels; congenital heart disease detection reached 0.956, and age was predicted within about 1.1 years on average.
- In a reader study, 17 clinicians reviewing 100 cases improved accuracy from 56.8% to 65.4% with AI help, and their accuracy did not drop on cases where the AI was wrong.

## Caveats
This is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed. Data come mainly from Chinese hospitals, so performance in other populations is unknown. High AUCs on retrospective labels do not prove better patient outcomes. The reader study was small.

## Key terms
- **Foundation model:** a large AI model pretrained broadly, then adapted to specific tasks.
- **Fine-tuning:** further training a pretrained model on a smaller, task-specific dataset.
- **AUC:** a 0–1 score of how well a model separates positive from negative cases.
- **12-lead ECG:** the standard hospital electrocardiogram recording the heart from 12 angles.
- **External validation:** testing on data from a different site than training.

items.title: With AI guidance, novices using handheld ultrasound caught severe aortic stenosis almost as well as sonographers
items.source: Yesil Science (on a Mayo Clinic study in JAMA Cardiology)
items.tldr: In 1,302 scans taken by untrained users with real-time AI coaching, the system detected severe aortic stenosis with 93% sensitivity, but needed cardiologist review to cut false alarms.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
A Mayo Clinic-led study, published in JAMA Cardiology and summarised by Yesil Science, tested whether people without imaging training could screen for severe aortic stenosis using a handheld ultrasound probe. AI guided them in real time on where to place the probe, then a second AI read the images.

## Why it matters
Severe aortic stenosis (a stiff, narrowed heart valve) is common in older adults and treatable with valve replacement, but many cases are found late. Formal echocardiography needs trained sonographers and is often scarce outside big centres. Novice-acquired screening could widen access in primary care or rural clinics.

## How it works
The interpretation model was built on 6,753 patients and validated at Mayo sites in Minnesota, Arizona and Florida.
- Retrospectively, it separated severe from non-severe stenosis with an AUC of 0.99.
- Of 1,302 exams acquired by novices, 96.6% were good enough for automated analysis.
- Sensitivity and specificity were 95% and 97% for sonographer scans, versus 93% and 96% for novice scans.
- Because severe stenosis is uncommon, only 49.4% of novice AI-positive results were true cases. When a cardiologist reviewed AI-positive scans, that positive predictive value rose to 91.1%.

## Caveats
All sites were within Mayo Clinic, so results may be better than in busy community clinics. The software on its own produces many false alarms, so a human review step is needed. The details here come from a secondary summary; the full paper should be checked before relying on specific numbers.

## Key terms
- **Aortic stenosis:** narrowing of the aortic valve that makes the heart work harder.
- **Handheld / point-of-care ultrasound:** a small probe connected to a phone or tablet.
- **Sensitivity / specificity:** share of true cases caught / share of non-cases correctly cleared.
- **Positive predictive value (PPV):** chance that a positive result is really a case; it falls when a disease is rare.
- **Real-time AI guidance:** on-screen prompts telling the user how to move the probe.

items.title: Menlo Ventures: US healthcare AI spending hits $3.7B as providers move past scribes
items.tldr: A survey of 550 US health executives says AI spending grew 2.5-fold in a year, with the fastest growth in clinical copilots and patient engagement, and big EHR vendors winning the scribe market.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
Venture firm Menlo Ventures released its second annual "State of AI in Healthcare" report. It estimates US healthcare AI spending at $3.7 billion in 2026, up 2.5 times from the year before. That makes healthcare the largest industry market for AI applications, ahead of legal ($1.8 billion).

## Why it matters
Health-system leaders are deciding where AI budgets go next. The report suggests money is shifting from back-office paperwork to tools that touch clinical decisions and patients, and that large incumbents are gaining ground on startups.

## Key details
- Providers (hospitals and practices) account for 77% of spending, about $2.9 billion.
- Clinical copilots (AI that answers clinical questions or suggests next steps) grew 5.5 times to $550 million; patient-engagement tools grew 4.5 times to $450 million.
- The ambient scribe market is about $950 million. Microsoft and Epic now hold 46% share, up from 33%, and won 68% of new scribe dollars.
- Life-sciences AI spending rose from $30 million to $700 million, and 51% of pharma companies say they run AI at scale, up from 15%.
- 43% of health plans say provider AI coding pushed up their 2026 medical cost trend; prior authorization is now the top payer AI priority (82%).
- The survey covered 550 director-level or higher buyers: 150 provider, 100 payer and 300 pharma/biotech executives.

## Caveats
This is an investor's report, and Menlo's portfolio includes Anthropic and OpenEvidence, which sell into this market. Spending figures are estimates from survey responses, not audited revenue. The press release does not list methods limits; the full report should be checked.

## Key terms
- **Ambient scribe:** AI that listens to a visit and drafts the clinical note.
- **Clinical copilot:** AI assistant that supports clinical reasoning or look-ups.
- **Revenue cycle / coding:** turning care into billing codes and claims.
- **Prior authorization:** insurer approval required before certain treatments.
- **EHR:** electronic health record system, such as Epic.

items.title: Provider survey: fewer patients abandon care over prior-auth delays, but trust in AI is becoming conditional
items.tldr: In a survey of 200 US hospital clinicians and administrators, the share reporting patients who dropped treatment because of authorization delays fell from 55% to 28%.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
Cohere Health, which sells prior-authorization software to health plans, released its second annual national provider survey, run with Wakefield Research. It polled 200 clinicians and office administrators at US hospitals and health systems.

## Why it matters
Prior authorization is one of the biggest administrative burdens in US care and a common cause of treatment delays. Insurers are adding AI to speed reviews, and regulators and states are watching whether AI is used to deny care. Provider trust shapes whether these tools are accepted.

## Key details
- Clinicians reporting that patients abandoned recommended treatment because of authorization delays fell from 55% last year to 28%.
- 96% of clinicians and 94% of administrators said they still trust AI in prior authorization, though the company describes that trust as increasingly conditional on transparency.
- Respondents reported fewer emergency visits and hospital stays linked to delays, but the release gives no figures.
- Cohere's chief medical officer, Brian Covino, stressed that AI should streamline paperwork and not be used to deny care.
- The full report is titled "Better AI, Not Less AI."

## Caveats
The survey was commissioned by a vendor whose product is AI prior authorization, and the sample is small (200) with no margin of error or sampling method reported. Only the clinician figure has a year-on-year comparison. Self-reported perceptions are not the same as measured delay times or outcomes.

## Key terms
- **Prior authorization:** insurer approval needed before a test, drug or procedure.
- **Health plan / payer:** the insurer that pays claims.
- **Treatment abandonment:** a patient not starting or stopping recommended care.
- **Vendor-commissioned survey:** a poll paid for by a company with an interest in the result.

items.title: Medicaid cuts push hospitals to demand faster, clearer returns from AI
items.tldr: Hospital CEOs and CFOs say looming Medicaid revenue losses mean AI projects must prove value within months, with some targeting 5–10x returns.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
At Becker's 14th annual CEO + CFO Roundtable in Chicago, hospital leaders described how federal Medicaid changes are reshaping AI budgets. DistilINFO summarised their remarks. The 2025 reconciliation law (HR 1) adds Medicaid work requirements in most states from 1 January 2027.

## Why it matters
Many hospitals bought AI tools during a period of easy pilots. With revenue under pressure, AI now competes with staffing and charity care for money. That changes which tools survive: those with measurable savings or revenue gains.

## Key details
- A Commonwealth Fund analysis of 2,958 acute-care hospitals projects operating-margin cuts of 11.7% to 13.3% in Medicaid expansion states, and revenue losses of $10.9–12.4 billion. Safety-net hospitals face cuts of about 26–30%.
- Cook County Health expects about $100 million in added charity-care costs for 2026–27.
- HonorHealth reviews each AI project 6–9 months after go-live to decide whether to keep it.
- Mount Sinai looks for 5–10 times return on technology spending.
- An Emory leader expects Epic's AI features to move to usage-based pricing by 2028; this is his view, not Epic policy.

## Caveats
These are executive remarks reported second-hand, not a systematic survey. The financial projections are modelled estimates, and some states may delay implementation. The article notes the figures are not directly comparable to each other.

## Key terms
- **Medicaid:** US public insurance for low-income people, run jointly by states and the federal government.
- **Operating margin:** revenue left after operating costs, as a share of revenue.
- **Safety-net hospital:** a hospital serving many uninsured or Medicaid patients.
- **ROI:** return on investment, the gain relative to cost.
- **Consumption pricing:** paying per use rather than a flat licence.

items.title: FDA starts saying 'super intelligence' instead of 'AI' in new documents; sponsors may keep using 'AI'
items.tldr: Under a September executive order, FDA's new public documents will use 'Super Intelligence (SI)', but existing AI guidance, submission rules and sponsors' wording stay the same.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
From 16 November 2026, FDA began replacing "artificial intelligence" and "AI" with "Super Intelligence" and "SI" in newly issued public documents, web pages and communications. The change implements Executive Order 14434, "Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence," signed on 29 September and published in the Federal Register on 2 October. Pink Sheet reported the same move, noting that sponsors can still say "AI."

## Why it matters
Regulatory affairs teams search FDA guidance, forms and databases by keyword. A change in wording can break saved searches, templates and internal policies. It also raises the question of whether a renamed term signals any change in how FDA reviews AI-based submissions.

## Key details
- The change applies only going forward; existing documents are not being re-issued.
- Current guidance, including Good Machine Learning Practice (GMLP) principles and predetermined change control plans (PCCPs), stays in force.
- Submission portals, eSTAR templates and 510(k), De Novo and PMA standards are unchanged.
- Both terms are accepted in filings. Companies do not need to rename products, relabel devices or revise dossiers.
- The statutory definition of AI in US law (15 U.S.C. 9401(3)) is unchanged.
- Web updates are expected in phases through early 2027, with related draft guidance possibly in early 2027.

## Caveats
The details come from CASRAI's summary, which relies on an FDA notice and law-firm alerts; the FDA notice itself should be checked. Law firms note the order binds federal agencies, not companies. Expect a period where both terms appear in FDA material.

## Key terms
- **Executive order:** a presidential directive to federal agencies.
- **GMLP:** Good Machine Learning Practice, shared principles for developing medical AI.
- **PCCP:** a pre-approved plan for how an AI device may be updated after clearance.
- **eSTAR:** FDA's electronic template for device submissions.
- **Sponsor:** the company submitting a product for approval.

items.title: Pharma quality leaders want a clear line between AI that needs full validation and AI that needs lighter controls
items.tldr: Industry panelists expect regulators to hold firms to their own internal AI policies and are waiting on a rumoured December regulatory AI playbook.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
PharmTech's weekly roundup focused on AI accountability in drug manufacturing and quality. Panelists discussed who is responsible when AI tools support regulated work, and what evidence regulators will expect.

## Why it matters
Drug makers increasingly use AI in batch record review, deviation handling, document drafting and pharmacovigilance. Under good manufacturing practice (GMP) rules, any computerised system that affects product quality must be validated. Over-validating every tool is costly, while under-validating risks inspection findings.

## Key details
- Panelists want regulators to separate high-risk AI uses that need full validation from lower-risk uses that need lighter controls.
- They expect inspectors to judge companies against the companies' own internal AI policies, so writing a policy and not following it becomes a compliance risk.
- Several expect a regulatory AI playbook in December; this is rumour, not an announced FDA document.
- The roundup also noted FDA's approval of asundexian, the first factor XIa inhibitor in the US, and reports that FDA has quietly shelved the Commissioner's National Priority Voucher pilot (an inference from press reports).

## Caveats
This is a trade-press roundup of interviews and panel views, not regulatory text. The timing of any playbook is speculative. Companies should anchor their plans on published guidance such as EU GMP draft Annex 22 and FDA's AI-in-drug-development guidance.

## Key terms
- **GMP:** good manufacturing practice, rules ensuring drugs are made consistently and safely.
- **Validation:** documented evidence that a system reliably does what it is meant to do.
- **Risk-based approach:** matching the level of control to the potential harm.
- **Factor XIa inhibitor:** a new class of blood thinner targeting a clotting protein.
- **Priority voucher:** a token granting faster FDA review.

items.title: Opinion: the regulatory window for AI in pharmacovigilance is open, and teams should start with case intake
items.tldr: A vendor-written piece lays out FDA, EMA and CIOMS positions on AI in drug safety monitoring and argues for a phased rollout starting with low-risk tasks.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
Ranga Gontina of IT firm Apexon argues that regulators have now said enough about AI in pharmacovigilance (drug safety monitoring) for companies to move from pilots to real use. The article pulls together the main guidance documents in one place.

## Why it matters
Safety teams process huge volumes of adverse-event reports; VigiBase, the WHO's global database, holds more than 40 million. AI can speed case intake and literature screening, but missed signals can harm patients. Knowing what regulators expect helps teams pick safe first uses.

## Key details
- FDA's January 2025 draft guidance on AI across the drug lifecycle asked for comments on pharmacovigilance uses; final guidance was expected around mid-2026.
- EMA published a reflection paper on AI in the medicines lifecycle in late 2024.
- CIOMS Working Group XIV issued a report in December 2025 with seven principles, including risk-proportionate oversight and clear human accountability.
- FDA and EMA released ten joint guiding principles for AI in drug development in January 2026.
- The author recommends a phased approach: start with case intake and literature screening, keep humans responsible for causality and signal decisions, then expand.

## Caveats
This is an opinion piece from a vendor, not regulatory text, and it is from July 2026, so the status of FDA's final guidance may have changed. Readers should go to the FDA, EMA and CIOMS documents directly.

## Key terms
- **Pharmacovigilance:** detecting and assessing side effects of medicines after approval.
- **Signal:** a possible new safety problem that needs investigation.
- **Case intake:** receiving and coding individual adverse-event reports.
- **CIOMS:** Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences, which writes consensus safety guidance.
- **Human-in-the-loop:** a person reviews or approves AI outputs before action.

items.title: AliveCor and PulseAI bring FDA-cleared AI rhythm reads to Apple, Samsung, Fitbit and Withings watches
items.tldr: PulseAI's 510(k)-cleared software will analyse single-lead watch ECGs inside AliveCor's Kardia app from early 2027, including beat-by-beat PVC detection on Apple Watch.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
AliveCor, maker of the Kardia ECG devices, partnered with Belfast-based PulseAI. PulseAI's "PulseAPI SmartWatch" software, which has FDA 510(k) clearance, will interpret ECGs recorded on third-party smartwatches for KardiaCare subscribers.

## Why it matters
Millions of people record ECGs on their watches, but built-in algorithms often return "inconclusive" results and detect only a few rhythms. A cleared, device-agnostic engine could give more usable results and route them into a care service. It also shows a growing model: AI software cleared separately from the hardware it runs on.

## How it works
The software is a library that analyses Lead I data (one electrical view of the heart) from compatible wearables.
- On Apple Watch it adds detection of premature ventricular contractions (PVCs), classifying each beat.
- It also gives rhythm determinations on Samsung Galaxy Watch, Fitbit Sense and Withings ScanWatch.
- The companies cite a prospective study of 296 people, published in Heart Rhythm, reporting better atrial fibrillation sensitivity than Apple's native algorithm and 92% fewer inconclusive readings.
- Availability is planned for the first half of 2027.

## Caveats
This is a company press release, and the 92% figure is company-reported; the full study citation was not provided. The 510(k) number is not given. A single-lead watch ECG cannot replace a 12-lead ECG for many diagnoses, and consumer use may increase follow-up visits for harmless findings.

## Key terms
- **510(k):** FDA clearance showing a device is substantially equivalent to one already marketed.
- **Single-lead ECG:** a heart recording from one pair of contact points, as on a watch.
- **PVC:** an extra heartbeat starting in the lower chambers; usually benign but sometimes significant.
- **Atrial fibrillation (AFib):** an irregular rhythm that raises stroke risk.
- **SaMD:** software as a medical device, software that is itself the regulated product.

items.title: FDA and MHRA officials signal draft generative-AI device policies within months
items.tldr: FDA's digital health chief said draft genAI guidance could come 'in the course of months', while the UK's MHRA plans draft change-control-plan guidance by year end.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
At The MedTech Conference in Boston, Rick Abramson, director of FDA's Digital Health Center of Excellence, and Jessica Paulsen, MHRA's deputy director for AI and software, discussed how both agencies plan to regulate devices built on generative AI (genAI), such as large language models.

## Why it matters
GenAI devices behave differently from classic locked algorithms: outputs vary, and they can be used for many tasks. Current clearance pathways struggle with that. Signals of upcoming policy help manufacturers plan evidence packages and update strategies.

## Key details
- In August, FDA published a discussion paper on a competency-based framework for genAI devices, using non-clinical benchmark testing plus clinical confirmation. It drew hundreds of comments.
- CDRH's fiscal 2027 guidance priorities include two genAI guidance documents.
- Abramson said manufacturers should expect draft policy "in the course of months," adding that FDA wants to move fast but not too fast.
- The MHRA accepted all 44 recommendations of the UK's National Commission on the Regulation of AI in Healthcare.
- The MHRA plans to publish draft guidance on predetermined change control plans (PCCPs) around the end of the year for consultation.

## Caveats
These are panel remarks, not formal commitments; dates may slip. Neither agency has published draft genAI device guidance yet. The article is from 20 October, so newer statements may exist.

## Key terms
- **Generative AI:** AI that produces text, images or other content, such as chatbots.
- **Competency-based framework:** judging a model by tested skills, similar to licensing a clinician.
- **PCCP:** a pre-authorised plan describing how an AI device can be changed after market entry.
- **MHRA:** the UK Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency.
- **CDRH:** FDA's Center for Devices and Radiological Health.

items.title: Medtech regulators shift from one-time approval to whole-lifecycle monitoring, driven by AI devices
items.tldr: Speakers at a Veeva summit in Amsterdam said regulators increasingly expect continuous monitoring before, during and after marketing, and most manufacturers are not ready.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
At the Veeva MedTech Summit in Amsterdam, panelists including Veeva's Amra Racic said device regulators are moving away from a single approval moment. Instead, they increasingly expect evidence across the whole product lifecycle. Medtech Insight reported the discussion.

## Why it matters
AI-enabled devices can change with updates and can drift as patient populations, scanners or clinical practice shift. A one-time clearance cannot capture that. Regulators such as FDA, the UK MHRA and EU notified bodies under the MDR and IVDR are therefore leaning on post-market data to keep products safe.

## Key details
- Panelists expect the push for continuous monitoring to grow through 2027.
- AI devices are the main driver, because their performance needs checking after launch.
- Most manufacturers lack the data systems and internal coordination (between regulatory, quality and clinical teams) to keep up.
- The trend links to tools already in place, such as predetermined change control plans in the US and post-market surveillance duties under EU rules.

## Caveats
The full article is behind a paywall; this summary is based on its published overview, so specific figures or regulator quotes were not available. These are conference views, not new rules. Companies should look at concrete requirements, such as EU MDR post-market surveillance and FDA PCCP guidance.

## Key terms
- **Lifecycle monitoring:** tracking a device's safety and performance from design through use.
- **Post-market surveillance:** collecting data on how a device performs after it is sold.
- **MDR / IVDR:** EU regulations for medical devices and in vitro diagnostics.
- **Notified body:** an organisation designated to assess device conformity in the EU.
- **Model drift:** declining AI performance as real-world data change.
